title: IR-2026-134 Lets Tax Pros Pay for Business Clients: Build the Firm-Wide Tax Pro Account Payment Register, Book Each Payment Type to the Right Liability, and Tie It Out Before the Next 941 Deposit
excerpt: IR-2026-134, issued November 6, 2026, lets authorized tax professionals make federal tax deposits, balance, extension, amended return, and proposed assessment payments for business clients through Tax Pro Account. Here is the firm-wide payment register, the journal entry for each of the five payment types, and the controls that keep a firm-initiated payment from becoming an unexplained ledger line.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Accounting firm payment register listing Tax Pro Account payments for twelve business clients by payment type, tax period, confirmation number, and ledger account
content:
Since November 6, 2026, an authorized tax professional can make federal tax deposits, balance, extension, amended return, and proposed assessment payments for business clients through Tax Pro Account. Before a firm uses it, build one payment register across clients, book each payment type to the right liability, and tie every confirmation to the client's bank and ledger.

Why this matters now

The IRS issued IR-2026-134 on 2026-11-06. It says authorized tax professionals can now make five kinds of payment on behalf of business clients through Tax Pro Account: full or partial balance, amended return, extension, proposed tax assessment, and federal tax deposit. Until now the service let a practitioner view a business client's balance and payment activity but not move money. The release adds one condition in one sentence: the professional must have the appropriate authorization for the client and the tax matters involved.

The Tax Pro Account service page, last updated 2026-10-30, now states that payments can be made on behalf of business clients and that power of attorney requests are limited to attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, and enrolled retirement plan agents. An earlier IRS tax tip dated 2026-06-18 describes the rest of the service: real-time CAF numbers, digital powers of attorney and tax information authorizations when both sides have accounts, and payments and payment plans within the scope of an authorization.

Trade coverage arrived the same day. The Journal of Accountancy and Accounting Today on 2026-11-06, and CPA Practice Advisor on 2026-11-09, each restate the five payment types and the authorization sentence. None of them say what a firm should get from the client before it pays, where each payment lands in the client's books, or how a firm with forty business clients proves every payment it made was the one it was asked to make. That is the gap this article fills, and the timing matters. The December 941 deposit cycle, year-end extension and balance planning, and the FIRE to IRIS transition all land in the next six weeks, and the first firm-initiated client payments will be made inside them.

What each of the five payment types means in the client's ledger

A payment through Tax Pro Account is a credit to the client's cash. The debit depends on what the payment settles, and the five types settle different things. The table gives the entry for a calendar-year business that accrues its liabilities. The IRS release does not describe the funding path, so confirm in the tool which account is debited before the first payment and never route client tax money through a firm account.

Payment type (IR-2026-134)What it usually settlesDebitCreditReviewer tie
Federal tax depositEmployment taxes already withheld and accrued through payroll (Form 941, Form 940)Federal withholding payable; FICA payable, employee and employer shareCashDeposit equals the payroll register liability for the period; payable goes to zero
Full or partial balanceTax shown on a filed return and not yet paid, or a notice balanceIncome taxes payable if accrued; income tax expense if not; penalties and interest on their own linesCashRemaining payable equals the IRS balance for that period after the payment
Extension paymentEstimated tax paid with Form 7004 before the return is filedIncome taxes payable to the extent accrued; prepaid income tax for any excessCashPrepaid balance reverses when the return is filed and the true-up is booked
Amended returnAdditional tax for a prior year, plus interestIncome tax expense (current period) or payable if a reserve existed; interest expense separatelyCashAmount agrees to the Form 1120-X or 941-X line for tax and the notice for interest
Proposed tax assessmentA notice amount the client has agreed to, split into tax, interest, and penaltyThe liability the tax relates to; interest expense; penalties, nondeductibleCashThree components reconcile to the notice; penalty line excluded from the tax return

Two accounting points sit behind the table. First, a federal tax deposit is never an expense at the date of payment. The expense was recognized when payroll ran, as a debit to wages and employer payroll tax expense and a credit to the liability accounts. The deposit reduces a point-in-time liability balance; it does not create a flow item. A client whose bank rule codes every IRS withdrawal to payroll tax expense double counts the employer share and leaves a phantom liability on the balance sheet.

Second, a proposed assessment is three transactions in one withdrawal. The tax component belongs to whatever liability the notice adjusts. The interest is interest expense. The penalty is an expense the client cannot deduct, and it belongs on its own account so the preparer can add it back without searching. A partnership or S corporation usually has no federal income tax of its own, so a balance due on its account is almost always penalty or interest, and booking it to owner draws or to income tax expense misstates the entity's results.

One firm, twelve business clients, one month: the walk-through

Call it Harbor Ledger CPAs: two partners, four staff, twelve business clients that have asked the firm to handle federal payments, and client books kept in separate QuickBooks Online files. The numbers are illustrative. The sequence is the point.

Step one: match each client's authorization to the tax matters the firm will pay

Before any payment, the firm lists every client, the authorization on file in Tax Pro Account, and the tax matters and periods it covers. Four clients have authorizations limited to income tax for 2024 and 2025. Those authorizations do not cover a 2026 Form 941 deposit, so the firm requests a new authorization for employment tax for 2026 before the first deposit and records the date it was accepted. The IRS release does not say which authorization scope is sufficient for which payment type. The firm's rule is simple: no payment for a tax matter or period the authorization does not name.

Step two: get the client's approval in writing, per payment

Each payment starts with a client approval that names the entity, the form, the tax period, the payment type, the amount, the funding account's last four digits, and the date by which it must settle. The approval is attached to the register row. A standing instruction to 'pay whatever is due' is not an approval of an amount, and the firm declines it. The engagement letter is amended to say the firm initiates payments only against a written approval and that the client remains responsible for funding the account.

Step three: make the payments and record four rows

During the month the firm makes four payments. For Cedar Mill Manufacturing, a C corporation, it makes a $18,400 federal tax deposit for the November 15 payroll: debit federal withholding payable $9,200, debit FICA payable $9,200, credit cash $18,400. The payroll register shows the same $18,400 of liability, and after the entry both payable accounts return to zero for the period.

For Pinehurst Dental PLLC, an S corporation, the firm pays a $645 proposed assessment on a late 941 deposit the client has agreed to: debit penalties, nondeductible $600, debit interest expense $45, credit cash $645. No tax component, because the deposit itself was already made. For Ridgeline Logistics, a C corporation, it makes a $25,000 extension payment for 2026 against an accrued income taxes payable of $21,000: debit income taxes payable $21,000, debit prepaid income tax $4,000, credit cash $25,000. For Harborview Apparel, a C corporation, it makes a $10,000 partial balance payment on 2025 tax of $14,000: debit income taxes payable $10,000, credit cash $10,000, leaving a $4,000 point-in-time payable that must agree to the IRS balance for that period.

Step four: tie out at month-end

At month-end a staff member who did not initiate the payments pulls three things for each client: the payment activity shown in Tax Pro Account, the bank statement withdrawals, and the ledger postings. Each register row must match on all three for amount, date, taxpayer, and period. Cedar Mill's $18,400 matches on all three. Ridgeline's bank shows $25,000 but the ledger shows a single $25,000 debit to income tax expense, posted by the client's bookkeeper from the bank feed. That is an exception: the entry is reclassified to payable and prepaid, and the client's bank rule is corrected. Pinehurst's $645 appears in the bank and the ledger but not yet in Tax Pro Account activity; the row stays open with a recheck date rather than being closed on two out of three.

The register itself is one table across all twelve clients: client, EIN last four, form and tax period, payment type, amount, approval reference, authorization reference, confirmation number, funding account last four, bank posting date, ledger reference, reviewer, and status. It is the same discipline as the vendor payment test run across every client: one register, one rule set, every client, every month. A firm that already keeps the register from an individual tax payment reconciliation extends it with the authorization and approval columns rather than starting over.

Accounting controls for firm-initiated client tax payments

Source data: the client's written approval for each payment; the authorization record in Tax Pro Account with its tax matters and periods; the payroll register or filed return that establishes the liability being paid; the IRS notice for any assessment, split into tax, interest, and penalty; the Tax Pro Account payment activity with confirmation numbers; the client's bank statement; and the client's ledger postings. Record the date each item was captured, and record IR-2026-134 and its 2026-11-06 date as the authority for the firm making the payment at all.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. For each row, confirm the authorization covers the tax matter and period. Confirm the approved amount equals the liability per the source document. Post the entry by payment type from the table above, with the credit always to cash and the debit to the liability, prepaid, expense, or penalty account the type calls for. At month-end, for each client, total the register's settled payments and agree that total to the sum of IRS withdrawals on the bank statement and to the sum of cash credits on the ledger coded to federal tax accounts. Compute each payable account's closing balance and agree it to the IRS balance for that period. Polarity: deposits and balance payments reduce liability balances, which are point-in-time; expense and penalty lines are flow items that belong to the period the notice is agreed, not the period the original return was filed.

Review: a second person at the firm, not the initiator, releases each payment against the approval and the authorization, then performs the month-end three-way match. The reviewer checks that no deposit was coded to expense, that every assessment is split three ways, that every prepaid balance has a return filing date it will reverse against, and that any row matching on fewer than three sources remains open with a next action. The partner reviews the open-item list monthly and the full register quarterly.

Decision: the client decides what to pay and when, and signs the approval. The firm decides whether the authorization on file permits it to act and whether the amount agrees to the source document; if either fails, it does not pay. The reviewer decides whether a row is closed. The partner decides whether the engagement letter and the authorization scope need to change. Nobody at the firm decides to pay an amount the client has not approved, however obvious the balance looks.

Limits and common mistakes

IR-2026-134 does not describe the funding path, limits, or cut-off times for business payments. Confirm them in the tool and do not assume Direct Pay rules for individuals apply unchanged.

An authorization to view is not an authorization to pay for every tax matter. The release ties the payment to the tax matters involved, so a 941 deposit needs employment tax within scope for the period, not just income tax.

A payment is a reduction of a liability, not evidence that the liability was right. Tie the deposit to the payroll register and the balance payment to the filed return. A register that ties cash to cash and skips the liability catches the wrong amount only after the notice arrives.

Do not close a row on two sources out of three. Tax Pro Account activity, the bank, and the ledger each answer a different question, and a missing one is an open item.

Bank feed rules are the most common source of error. A rule that codes IRS withdrawals to one expense account will misstate payroll liabilities, prepaid tax, and nondeductible penalties in the same month. Review the client's rules before the firm starts paying, using the same approach as a custom automation control checklist.

Harbor Ledger CPAs and its clients are illustrative. The payment types, the authorization condition, the quotation, and the dates come from the IRS and trade sources cited above.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did IR-2026-134 change about Tax Pro Account?

On November 6, 2026, the IRS announced that authorized tax professionals can make full or partial balance, amended return, extension, proposed tax assessment, and federal tax deposit payments on behalf of business clients through Tax Pro Account. Before the change, practitioners could view a business client's balance and payment activity but could not make a payment. The professional must have the appropriate authorization for the client and the tax matters involved.

How should a federal tax deposit made through Tax Pro Account be recorded in the client's books?

Debit the payroll liability accounts the deposit settles, federal withholding payable and FICA payable for both the employee and employer share, and credit cash. The expense was already recognized when payroll ran. The deposit reduces a point-in-time liability balance, and after the entry the payable for that period should return to zero and agree to the payroll register.

Is a proposed tax assessment payment an expense?

Only partly. Split the notice into tax, interest, and penalty. The tax component is debited to the liability the notice adjusts, the interest to interest expense, and the penalty to a nondeductible penalties account so it can be added back on the return. A partnership or S corporation usually owes no federal income tax of its own, so a balance on its account is almost always penalty or interest.

What authorization does a tax professional need to pay for a business client?

IR-2026-134 says the professional must have the appropriate authorization for the client and the tax matters involved, and the Tax Pro Account page limits power of attorney requests to attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, enrolled actuaries, and enrolled retirement plan agents. A practical rule is to make no payment for a tax matter or period that the authorization on file does not name, and to get the client's written approval of the amount, type, and period for each payment.

How does a firm reconcile Tax Pro Account payments across many clients?

Keep one register across all clients with the client, form and period, payment type, amount, approval and authorization references, confirmation number, bank posting date, ledger reference, reviewer, and status. At month-end a person who did not initiate the payments matches each row to Tax Pro Account activity, the bank statement, and the ledger, agrees each payable account's closing balance to the IRS balance for the period, and leaves any row that matches on fewer than three sources open with a next action.

Once every client's federal payments sit in one register with a liability they settle and a confirmation that proves it, the firm can answer the partner's question for any client in seconds.
